speechtext: I should like to address a question to the Minister of Finance, which is dealt with in part, but only in part, by his own statement earlier today. Bearing in mind current reports concerning widespread epidemics of influenza in other countries, what research is being done in Canada with a view to the prevention and control of this disease?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The Department of National Health and Welfare is working in close co-operation with the world health organization in the early recognition of clinical influenza and the detection of the particular strain of virus prevalent during an epidemic of this disease. The advance notice of the presence of influenza in one or more countries is, of course, most important, as it is hoped that other countries will then have sufficient time to produce and administer vaccine containing the current strain of influenza. In this way, key personnel and particularly susceptible individuals may be protected. Influenza vaccine is only effective where the current strain or a closely associated strain of virus is included in the vaccine.

This winter the Department of National Health and Welfare is co-operating with the Department of National Defence in establishing a field trial to assess the protective value of influenza vaccine. About 7,000 doses of vaccine including some control material have been distributed across Canada. These have been allocated by provincial health officers to industrial groups, hospital staffs, etc., and by the Department of National Defence to various R.C.A.F. stations. As this vaccine contains a strain of influenza virus which is similar to the current strain now prevalent in other countries, it is expected that this trial will provide an accurate evaluation of the protective qualities of influenza vaccine.

board recommended and the governor in council approved the present vice-president's appointment effective by order in council P.C. 5156, dated October 25,	1950. The
Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) informed the house of these orders in council, among others, and I am tabling copies herewith.
When dealing with the matter of salaries, last Thursday, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), as reported on page 2090, stated it was his understanding that certain men in the corporation have raised their salaries. This statement creates an erroneous impression. These gentlemen have not raised their salaries nor can they do so. It is clear from the act that salaries of the president and vice-president are fixed by the board of the corporation, with the approval of the governor in council.
On this matter of salaries, hon. members may be interested to know that the president's salary remained unchanged from the date of his first appointment on January 1, 1946, until his reappointment as of January 1. 1953, when it was increased approximately 11 per cent. The salary of the vice-president has not been changed since he was appointed on October 25, 1950. With respect to other employees or officers of the corporation, I must refer as I did on Thursday last to section 14 (1) of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act, which states that:
The corporation may on its own behalf employ such officers and employees for such purposes and on such terms and conditions as may be determined by the executive committee and such officers and employees are not officers or servants of His Majesty.
The government does not therefore have available to it the information on salaries of such officers and employees. When the legislation was enacted in 1945 it was the expressed wish of parliament that this section should apply and I am therefore not in a position to make this information available.
I am not clear as to the reason for requesting copies of all cheques made during the months of December 1952 and January 1953 as requested in this notice of motion. These are accounting documents, and it has not been the practice to ask crown corporations to produce them. I recall that the same hon. member put a similar notice on the order paper in 1950 with respect to a certain officer of the Canadian National Railways. At that time the matter was dealt with by my colleague, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), who explained why it was not possible then to make the information available.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the principle governing the relationship between crown corporations and parliament was first enunciated on April 26, 1920, by Hon. Arthur Meighen, then minister of the interior, who said in part, as reported at page 1665 of Hansard of that year when explaining why certain information could not be made available:
... it Is utterly inconceivable that a tremendous aggregation of railways, a great system such as the Canadian National system has now grown to be, could ever be conducted along that line. I do not think that there is one hon. member in this house who would rise in his place and suggest that it could appeal to his mind for a moment that any such system of management could be made a success for a single day.
He was speaking then of the corporate system and its relationship to parliament; that is, of course, a corporate system such as what we know as a crown company for the purposes of this return. That argument was repeated effectively by Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, who was then prime minister, on March 22, 1921, as found at page 1181 of Hansard of that year; and I recommend both these speeches to the attention of hon. members who are interested.
In the light of the explanation I have just made, Mr. Chairman, I do not believe that hon. members would wish me to go contrary to the specific terms of the legislation enacted by parliament covering this corporation. I therefore regret that I am unable to produce everything requested. However, 1 suggest that the hon. member may obtain much of the information he is seeking by referring to the orders in council which I have mentioned and which have now been tabled.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION OF ACT FROM MAY 31, 1953 TO MAY 31, 1954

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, February 20, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. St. Laurent-Mr. Beaudoin in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Emergency Powers Act to provide for the continuation of the act for a further period of one year, that is from the thirty-first day of May, 1953, to the thirty-first day of May, 1954.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION OF ACT FROM MAY 31, 1953 TO MAY 31, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the time
the Emergency Powers Act was sought in 1951 by the present government, the law had been continuously for a period of 37 consecutive years that in an emergency of apprehended war the government could invoke the virtually unlimited powers of the War Measures Act. Rather than do so we came to this house in 1951 seeking the passage of a measure granting us much more limited powers and subject to greater parliamentary control.
This course was at that time approved by every party in the house. The resolution introducing it was passed without division. First and second readings of the bill were passed without division. Third reading was passed upon division, and in that way it became law. My statements previously made

Emergency Powers Act to this effect have been challenged by the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Kamloops. When they were so challenged, making allowance for the fact that there can be differences of opinion even with regard to matters of fact, I sat here with the proof of the accuracy of my statements in my possession and said nothing. But then the Leader of the Opposition got up and supported these charges that my statements were inaccurate, and I have also found a report in the Montreal Star of February 10 last of a meeting in Westmount-St. Antoine at which the hon. member for Nanaimo is reported as having said the following:
Canada today is living on the "edge of a dictatorship" and Canadians dare not take one more step "along the road to Moscow," Major General George R. Pearkes, V.C., member of parliament for Nanaimo, told the Westmount-St. Antoine Progressive Conservative Association in Victoria Hall last night.
Then he is reported as going on to say this:
The government's introduction of the Emergency Powers Act last week to replace the War Measures Act showed that there was a drift away from parliamentary control and that the cabinet was usurping the power of parliament. "Once the government concedes that certain powers are necessary and takes it on itself to administer the country without reference to parliament, to pass a large number of measures by order in council, the lust for power grows and they hate to surrender the powers they have taken unto themselves, even though the emergency is long past."

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION OF ACT FROM MAY 31, 1953 TO MAY 31, 1954
speechtext: Another of my excellent speeches.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION OF ACT FROM MAY 31, 1953 TO MAY 31, 1954
speechtext: Making allowance for the fact that of course errors can creep into journalistic reports of meetings of that sort, it is apparent that the report is patently wrong in two respects. The act was not introduced at that time, and far from there having been a large number of orders in council passed under it, the very opposite is true. Member after member of the official opposition has risen in his place and complained not about the large numbers of orders in council but about the very small numbers.

speechtext: There was never any complaint.

When he sat down he was followed by the Leader of the Opposition who pro-

ceeded, also in the most explicit language, to agree completely with the Prime Minister upon four points.

speechtext: No, that is all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION OF ACT FROM MAY 31, 1953 TO MAY 31, 1954
speechtext:
First of all he agreed that we were in the emergency of apprehended war as stated by the Prime Minister; if he wishes me to do so I will quote Hansard to him, but he must remember what he said. Second, he said it was not desirable to invoke the War Measures Act, and thereby to create the impression in the minds of the Canadian people that war was inevitable. Hence third, the Leader of the Opposition agreed with the Prime Minister that the War Measures Act should not be invoked; in place of that he suggested, fourth, the following, to use his own language as found at page 500:
... I wish to indicate my own support for the proposition now placed before us that such emergency measures as are to be adopted shall be brought clearly before parliament and shall be the results of actual decisions of members of this house.
Well, Mr. Chairman, that is precisely what has been done. Certain sections of the Emergency Powers Act, as they are now upon the statute books, are in their present form as a result of suggestions made by members of the official opposition as to the form those sections should take. The members in question were the hon. member for Kamloops and the hon. member for Eglinton. In the face of these expressed statements of the Leader of the Opposition, it seems to me a most extraordinary proposition that he should now say that he was opposed to the legislation at that time.
But, sir, that is by no means all. At that time the thinking of the Leader of the Opposition (upon this subject was dominated- and I think that is not too strong a word to use-like that of the members of the C.C.F. party, by the idea that we should have a complete system of wage and price controls in this country. I put it to any of the legal members of the Conservative party in the house that we could not have a complete system of wage and price controls unless the government had emergency powers. If, therefore, as the Leader of the Opposition stated, he was opposed to our invoking emergency powers under the War Measures Act, then it was absolutely essential, in order to carry into effect his own policy of wage and price controls, that the government should have emergency powers of some kind. As he had said in the language I quoted a

moment ago that such emergency powers "as are to be adopted shall be brought clearly before parliament and should be the results of actual decisions of members of this house", it was perfectly clear that the only possible way in which his own idea about wage and price controls could be given effect to was by a measure of the precise kind which we are now discussing.

Let my hon. friend listen to this and tell us what he meant by it if he did not mean that controls should be put into effect at once. -the sooner these controls are put in the better it is going to be for all Canadians.

speechtext:
Of course, I shall correct the
minister when I speak but the minister knows perfectly well that he is misinterpreting the facts. If he will read above he will see perfectly clearly the controls I had in mind.

speechtext:
I was in the house when
these statements were made in the first place by my hon. friend in that debate. I also recollect when he was denying these things a few days ago. I went back to Hansard, all I could do, and, from it I have read the English language. If my hon. friend can get up and interpret, from the language which I have read, anything other than that he wanted wage and price controls to be put in, then he is a much more ingenious man than I have ever taken him to be.
There is nothing to be ashamed of in advocating wage and price controls. My hon. friends, the members of the C.C.F. party, have consistently done so and if I am not mistaken they would probably urge them still. But there is a difference between the C.C.F party and the Conservative party for which we must give the C.C.F. party credit for the fact that political doctrines theiy believe in on Monday, they still believe in on Tuesday. What they believe in in January they still support in December.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION OF ACT FROM MAY 31, 1953 TO MAY 31, 1954

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION OF ACT FROM MAY 31, 1953 TO MAY 31, 1954
speechtext:
When they come into this present debate they say they do not wish to extend the Emergency Powers Act. Why? Because we have not used these powers to put in price controls-which is a good, fair, honest reason. But my hon. friends of the Conservative party, in view of an election being imminent, now want to go out and take advantage of the fact that the government has a large majority-to make virtue out of necessity-by saying that this government is a great dictatorship; that it is taking away the powers of the people; that it is engaging in a great conspiracy to destroy the supremacy of parliament-and the like.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, and I hope I may use this word within parliamentary rules, that my hon. friends of the Conservative party have a good deal of effrontery here

Emergency Powers Act to come and deny what their position was on the Emergency Powers Act when, in order to give effect to the central part of my hon. friend's speech to put in a system of wage and price controls, it was absolutely essential for the government to have emergency powers and, within the terms of my hon. friend's own statement, emergency powers of the precise character of those we are now discussing.
My hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition quoted from his speech and I have quoted from it. There is no difficulty there because, as always, it is a very long speech and his remarks upon price controls alone would make a large speech in themselves. They begin at the top of the second column of page 503 of Hansard of February 20, 1951, take the whole of that column, the whole of page 504, the whole of page 505, the whole of page 506, and they end on page 507. Now, my hon. friend says that he never did any such thing, that he does not remember making a speech of that sort at all.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION OF ACT FROM MAY 31, 1953 TO MAY 31, 1954
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION OF ACT FROM MAY 31, 1953 TO MAY 31, 1954
speechtext: Nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION OF ACT FROM MAY 31, 1953 TO MAY 31, 1954
speechtext:
Let me remind him of what
he said. He opened up with a column-no, a column and a half-in which he quoted his favorite authority, himself, at great length. Then, having tired of that, he quoted at great length from a speech made by Donald Gordon about two weeks before that date in Montreal. Then, when he finished with that matter, he quoted from a speech made by Walter L. Gordon of Toronto. It was a speech in which Mr. Gordon, as I said, not only indicated the wisdom of having a policy of wage and price controls but stated the commodities on which those controls should be placed and the levels at which they should be imposed.
Then my hon. friend's conscience was bothering him and he was worried about where he stood in relation to free enterprise and he was groping around for some way out and he found it in the United States. At page 505 he said:
-may I point out that in the United States- which has been regarded by most people in most parts of the world as the great home of free enterprise-the two men who are mainly responsible for price and other controls are two men who, I would imagine, would be .generally regarded as the very top-level examples of success under the free enterprise system. I would point out that the two men who have been charged with responsibility, and have accepted it, for exercising controls in the United States are Charles E. Wilson and Eric Johnston. Both of them have wide and extensive experience and both have been lifelong exponents of the free enterprise system.
So, Mr. Chairman, this was an enterprise into which any good Conservative could go 

with the feeling that he was in a respectable enterprise and not a socialistic one. Now, he goes on again at page 505. He tells us just now that he was not in 1951 advocating immediate control. But at page 505 of Hansard he is recorded as having stated:

The Minister of Justice has not yet attempted to deal with what is the most important consideration with respect to the proposal now before us. We are asked to declare that it is expedient that this bill be re-enacted. For several days now we have


been trying to find out why it is expedient. What we have asked and what we are asking again is why is it expedient that this bill be re-enacted in view of the wide powers this legislation contains as interpreted by the judgment of the privy council.
What is most disturbing about the attitude of the government toward the resolution now before us is the complete failure of the government to deal with the entirely different effect of the legislation as the result of the judgment last year of the privy council in what is known as the Nolan case. It is true that the wording may be the same, but the effect of every important law which remains on the statute books for any length of time ultimately finds its interpretation in the judgment of the courts. When that judgment comes from the court of last resort, whether it was the privy council last year or, now, the Supreme Court of Canada, that judgment then becomes a precedent which the courts will follow when at any time in the future they are called upon to interpret the same law.
As an example, in seeking an interpretation of our basic constitution, the British North America Act, we must not only examine the words of the act itself but also the long series of judgments which interpret the effect of different sections of that act, and particularly that extremely important section of the act which confers upon the provinces exclusive jurisdiction over property and civil rights. Anyone seeking to determine the dividing line between the responsibility of dominion and provincial governments, and legislative bodies of which they are the executive under sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act, must examine the cases which have been tried and examine the judgments in order to see what the real effect of those sections has been found to be. The same is true of the preamble to the British North America Act and of many other important sections of it. In a number of cases they have been given a judicial interpretation quite contrary to that which they were assumed to have in the early days.
The same is equally true of the legislation which we are now asked to declare should be re-enacted by this parliament. How far does this legislation go? It is not enough to say: Here is the act, and it tells you. It is necessary to take the act and also to examine the judgments under the act, and related judgments, to find out what the words actually mean.
In the judgment in the Nolan case, referred to already in this debate, we were told that the courts must be ready to accept the

proposition that there was in fact an emergency which justified the action of the government, for the government had so declared by an order passed under that act. Moreover, it has been declared in that case that the courts are not in a position to review the circumstances which might or might not have justified the nature of the order made.
The Nolan case indicated the importance of this proposition. That was a case where it was alleged before the courts of Manitoba on behalf of a man named Nolan that the circumstances did not in fact constitute an emergency such as could be contemplated by the act and that, moreover, what had been done was contrary to the general purposes of the act. In that case grain had been seized and certain steps had been taken under an order which was intended to prevent Mr. Nolan making profits out of prices which had been fixed by the government under its controls-and, I might say, all this by the government which is now professing such an objection to controls of any kind. In one case the government does not hesitate to have price controls-since the war-and in another case it raises a great clamour about even suggesting that price controls might have been exercised.
This is a case where a price control was exercised. Not only was there a price control exercised, but the government decided that they were not going to permit an individual or individuals to make a substantial profit from that fact. Now, whether it was desirable or not that any profit be made, the question before the courts was whether this did in fact cross the boundary into the areas of property and civil rights reserved to the provinces under the British North America Act and whether, also, the facts were such as to justify an order of that kind.
So far as the Manitoba courts and the Supreme Court of Canada were concerned, Mr. Nolan's position was upheld; but in the privy council the position was reversed, and that is now the law. That law has been stated perfectly clearly and that law is what now tells us what this act really means. This law has been already read into the record, so it is not necessary to repeat it beyond referring again to the effect of that judgment in interpreting the power of the act now before us. That judgment of the privy council found:
-that it was not competent for the courts to canvass the considerations which had led the governor in council to deem it necessary to effect the vesting, or to ascribe to the order in council a purpose other than that which it professed to serve; the measures authorized were such as the governor in council, not the courts, deemed necessary or advisable.
Emergency Powers Act
Then the judgment went on to interpret the effect of the other words contained in this act as giving these wide powers which give almost unrestrained authority to the government under the act now before us.
The history of the interpretation of emergency legislation of this kind is one of ever-increasing power on the part of the dominion government, not only at the expense of parliament but at the expense of the provincial legislatures and the provincial governments. The first great milestone in the interpretation of the scope of legislation of this nature, and orders passed under it, was the Fort Frances Pulp and Paper Company case. In that case the Manitoba Free Press Company sought a declaration that an order affecting newsprint was ultra vires. There had been an order made under the War Measures Act, and the effect of that order had been continued after the war. The Manitoba Free Press Company sought to have this order declared ultra vires and to recover certain moneys that had been paid. That case went to the privy council and the judgment is to be found in Appeal Cases, 1923, page 695, under the title "Fort Frances Pulp and Paper Company Limited, appellants, and Manitoba Free Press Company Limited, and others, respondents". The effect of the judgment is to be found in these words at page 706:
It may ba that it has become clear that the crisis which arose is wholly at an end and that there is no justification for the continued exercise of an exceptional interference which becomes ultra vires when it is no longer called for. In such a case the law as laid down for distribution of powers in the ruling instrument would have to be invoked. But very clear evidence that the crisis had wholly passed away would be required to justify the judiciary, even when the question raised was one of ultra vires which it had to decide, in overruling the decision of the government that exceptional measures were still requisite.
In that case, Mr. Chairman, the arguments related to the extent to which the powers or jurisdiction of the provincial legislature might be overridden, and actually the judgment undoubtedly gave a wider interpretation to the emergency powers than had, up to that time, been in people's minds. From that time onward, however, that judgment did indicate the wide powers that existed under the emergency legislation, legislation very similar to that now before us. This judgment was followed in a number of cases in the intervening years.
Then we come to the second milestone, which is a case decided last year by the privy council under the title "The Attorney General of Canada and another, appellants, and Hallet and Carey Limited and another, respondents", as reported at page 427 of 1952 Appeal Cases. This case is generally known as the Nolan
2308	HOUSE OF
Emergency Powers Act case because Mr. Nolan was the man who actively carried that case forward.
Now, Mr. Chairman, when we have that interpretation before us I submit that it is the duty of the government to explain why an emergency act of this kind is required at this time; and it is also the duty of the members of parliament not to abdicate their position of supreme responsibility without some explanation from the Minister of Justice or the government as to why such wide powers are necessary. We have been told that the government prefers to tell us exactly what it is intending to do. This government has not told us what it is going to do. This government has not indicated in any way the kind of situation it thinks it would be called upon to deal with under this act which it now asks us to say should be brought before us.
It does seem difficult to understand the unwillingness of the government to indicate to us or to the people of Canada a single reason why this act, with its wider powers under the interpretation given, should be carried forward. We have been told that this act spells out what the government will do. It spells out nothing. It asks for a blank cheque. The only reservations contained in the measure are of a most illusory nature. These are the reservations in section 2. I repeat that so far as arrest is concerned, the only reservation is that it must not be arrest except as incidental to something done under this act.
If anything is ordered to be done under this act and anyone fails to comply with that order, then there is no exception in this act to the powers of arrest. Censorship or the control and suppression of publications and writings-how much does that mean when this government, under an order, can withhold from any newspaper or any publication the paper on which to print either the newspaper or the publication? It is not enough to say that this government would not do it. They could do it. They did something of that kind in the case of the Eldorado Mining company when they picked that particular mining company and said they were going to take it over. They could take over any newspaper or publishing house in precisely the same way. It is not enough to say that this government would not do it. The power is there.
That is the second exception. The third concerns the expenditure of money otherwise than in accordance with appropriation by parliament, except the expenditure of money from any fund or amount established by order or regulation in connection with a
Mr. Drew.]

scheme of control for the purposes of that scheme of control. Since all production, transportation, communication and other human activity comes under the possible application of this act, plans could be made relating to the whole economic and personal activity of this country and, within the meaning of this act, appropriations could be made without reference to parliament for any of the plans made to carry out those controls. In fact I submit that, by the ordinary rules of interpretation, the very inclusion of this exception implies that there is power to raise the money once the government has settled on a plan which needs a sum of money to carry it out.
I submit also that there are practically no reservations whatever in this act, and that the whole productive and economic life of this country is brought fully under the powers of this act without definition of the terms under which those powers can be exercised. In effect that was what the Prime Minister said last Friday. When we are given a lecture by the Minister of Justice in the way he delivered one to us this afternoon, exactly what occurred on Friday night should be recalled. The hon. member for Lake Centre was seeking some clarification of certain points in this act. He asked the Minister of Justice if it was not so that, under this act, certain things could be done. Each one of those things was quite clear, and there was not the slightest doubt as to what were the powers of this act in relation to them. The Minister of Justice, as recorded at page 2278 of Hansard for February 20, 1953, had this to say:
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend has practised law for many years. I think if a client came to him and asked him the question he has just asked me he would want two weeks to give an opinion upon it, and he would not give that opinion until he had given the question the most mature consideration.
Then the hon. member for Lake Centre said that, for the convenience of the Minister of Justice, he would break it down into single questions. He started to do so, and at that point the Prime Minister had this to say, as reported on the same page of Hansard:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I may be more venturesome than the minister. I would venture to say that if those things are things that could be done by parliament, they would be transferred by this act, as regards power, to the government. But they would not be any more apt to be exercised by the government than they would be apt to be exercised by parliament.
The Prime Minister had no doubt about what the act meant, and the Minister of Justice should have had no doubt because he is one who has been asking us to accept this act. If he has not yet studied the act

he has no right to be pressing us to adopt the resolution which says it is expedient that this act be continued. We have a clear statement from the Prime Minister that if these things are things that could be done by parliament they would be transferred by this act, as regards power, to the government. There is no question about it.
Subject to these illusory reservations in section 2 to which I have referred, this act places the whole economic and personal life of this country under the government, subject only to such measure of restraint as they choose to exercise. But we have been told that this act, of course, has a sound provision which safeguards parliament and the public. We are told that this act provides that the orders must be tabled. This act tells us that the orders must be laid before parliament within five days after the making of a regulation if it is made by the governor in council and within fifteen days in the case of any other regulation; or if parliament is not then in session, within a like period after the commencement of the next ensuing session thereof.
Mr. Chairman, it is necessary to repeat a reference to this matter because the minister has not yet sought in any way to deal with the point which has been made and which cannot be challenged, namely that it is possible for this or any other government to withhold publication of the orders under that provision; and again, it is only the discretion of the government that operates. The Regulations Act, which calls for publication of the regulations, under section 9 says explicitly that the government may exempt from publication any regulation it has passed. That is a wide and dangerous power which should not be available to any government, no matter how high and lofty the intentions and principles of that government may be. The fact that a government is made up of men who do not seek deliberately to abuse the powers they have is no answer to the fact that there are conferred powers which are contrary to the fundamental principles of parliament.

What should be remembered is this, and it does not seem to have yet impressed the Minister of Justice because he has not dealt with it in any way. We are not merely dealing with an emergency act of this kind as though it came before Westminster, where there is only one parliament to deal with it and where the right of review might have some effect. We are a federal parliamentary democracy; and when an order of this kind is passed which abridges the ordinary reservation to the provinces of property and civil rights, by passing a secret order of that kind and imposing a ban of secrecy upon it, the government is not only challenging the authority of parliament, but is also taking authority to deny the provincial legislatures and provincial governments any right to deal with this matter.
I repeat that whatever doubtful rights may be available under this act

and they are only imaginary rights under the Emergency Powers Act-or whatever supposed rights there may be, those rights are not available to the provincial governments or to members of the legislatures. Therefore this act, hand in hand with the Defence Production Act and the Regulations Act, suspends our constitution and leaves the provincial legislatures, the provincial governments and the members of this parliament entirely at the mercy of any government in power during the life of legislation of this nature.
The fact that there has been only one secret order, or so we are informed-although not one of us knows anything about the operation of it-does not indicate any protection to parliament and to the provincial legislatures. It merely indicates that the government is prepared to enshroud its secret act by the cloak of still further secrecy and to deny the operation of the Emergency Powers Act so far as review is concerned. If it is prepared to do that in one case, why is it not prepared to do it in any other case if it should come to the conclusion that such a step would be in the interest either of the public or of the government?
Mr. Speaker, it is not so much wrongdoing under an act that is the concern of members of parliament. Our task is to pass laws that do not permit wrongdoing. When we pass laws which create an offence, we do not say, "Tell us about the offence first and then we will deal with it by specific legislation". We are told that the rights of society demand

The Emergency Powers Act was introduced into the house by a resolution in connection with which the Prime Minister gave a fairly lengthy explanation of the very point which my hon. friend has now raised. He made it clear then, to the expressed approval of the leaders of the three opposition parties which I quoted earlier this afternoon, that in 1951 we had had the War Measures Act on our statute books for a period of some 37 years, with virtually unlimited powers which could be invoked to deal with the emergency of apprehended war. He said, however, that the government had considered it a preferable alternative to bring to parliament in the Emergency Powers Act a statute which would be passed by parliament, and the powers of which parliament would approve; that that statute would provide for the prompt tabling of the orders in council passed under it, and for proper machinery whereby members of parliament can seek annulment of those acts or orders in council passed by the government under the Emergency Powers Act with which for one reason or another they might disagree. It was perfectly clear from the debate at that time that the course met with the approval of all of the opposition parties.
At the present time we are considering whether or not the Emergency Powers Act should be extended for another twelve months. My hon. friend asked me the other night to state under what set of circumstances we might likely need the powers granted under the Emergency Powers Act. I have endeavoured before-I must confess without great measure of success-to make this point clear, and I will make another attempt now. If we knew with some exactitude the sets of unforeseen facts that we shall encounter during the next twelve months we would not need to have stand-by emergency powers at all; if we could be perfectly certain that such and such things were going to take place, obviously the proper course would be to bring in a bill to provide in adequate detail for things we knew were going to happen; and we would not need emergency powers. The essential character of emergency powers is that they

empower the government to deal with unforeseen circumstances which it is anticipated may arise during the emergency but the nature of which circumstances cannot be forecast in advance.
The whole idea of the War Measures Act, for example, is that when there is war real or apprehended it is pretty difficult to deal with some of the exigencies-sudden invasion, for example-by calling parliament together and debating the matter, something which would take some days. The idea of the War Measures Act is that the government, to deal with these exigencies, will have power to act at once. As X said in a previous reply to my hon. friend, it might be in a matter of hours or a matter of minutes.
When members of the opposition say, and I am making the suggestion with great respect and deference, "Why won't you tell us just what you need this for", that question indicates that they do not completely comprehend the nature of emergency powers. Emergency powers are given to deal with circumstances which we cannot foresee, if and when they arise. In relation to our present situation, some time before August, 1954, we must have, according to law, a general election. If the position is taken by my hon. friends of every opposition party- I do not know whether they all still take it. but they took it in 1951-that they would much prefer we should use the Emergency Powers Act than the War Measures Act, then we have to have the emergency powers which are available to us under the Emergency Powers Act in order to deal, for example, with an invasion; or to deal with questions, for instance, arising out of a shortage of freight cars, and other matters of that sort which cannot be foreseen in advance.

The question asked by the hon. member for York South was whether there had been any emergency in which it was necessary to invoke these powers. The minister said, as recorded at page 2281 of Hansard for February 20, 1953:
In reply to my hon. friend's question, may I say that the orders in council that have been passed themselves indicate that no fact has arisen during the past years which would make the possession of the powers covered by this statute absolutely essential.
I think that statement in itself is very convincing evidence that, with the situation as it has been in the world during the past two years, there have been no facts which have made it necessary to pass any orders in council under these powers. I do not see, therefore, why this act should be necessary at all.
The minister went on to state that the great necessity for the act was that in case the house were dissolved, and between the time of the dissolution of the house and the time a new government was elected some emergency should arise through war in Asia or some other part of the world, it would be necessary for us to have these emergency powers. That is the meaning I took from the statement the minister made. He said also that the War Measures Act, which we have on the statute books and which to my mind would deal with a situation of that kind, would be too drastic to use.
With the situation in the world as it is today, there has been so far no necessity for the Emergency Powers Act. The minister believes it is necessary to place this act on the statute books to cover the few weeks during which there might be no elected parliament. In that case, Mr. Chairman, we would have not only the Emergency Powers Act but we would have also the War Measures Act, both available at the same time.
I am satisfied that in case of actual war such as the minister outlined, instead of


passing orders in council under the Emergency Powers Act the government would invoke the War Measures Act. They could use the War Measures Act as much or as little as they thought necessary to meet the situation.
I should like to quote the War Measures Act to indicate that, in my opinion, it would meet the situation as outlined by the minister. Section 3 reads as follows:
The governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things and make from time to time such orders and regulations, as he may by reason of the existence of real or apprehended war, invasion or insurrection, deem necessary or advisable for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada.
By invoking that act, Mr. Chairman, at a time such as the minister mentioned, I am sure it would cover the situation and there would be no necessity for the Emergency Powers Act at all. My point is this. Why continue another act in peacetime which the minister claims might only be necessary in time of war? I think that is a fair statement to make and a fair inference to draw from what the minister said on Friday last.
Then another fact which might be presented with reference to these emergency powers is that so few orders in council have been passed under these powers since they have been in force. In 1951, for instance, there were 17 orders in council, and I understand that none of them was of very great importance. In 1952 there were five orders in council. I am not going to deal with those orders in council to any extent tonight. They have been dealt with by hon. members who have spoken previously. I believe three of them were revoked; one had to do with seamen on the great lakes, and the other had to do with private or ham radio stations, as we call them. Both these matters could have been dealt with by amendments to other acts.
Those are the facts which appeal to me as quite definite proof that emergency powers are not needed by this government at the present time. Having an act such as this in peacetime, as has been pointed out on so many occasions by previous speakers, is in my opinion an infringement of the rights of the people.
We may perhaps belittle the struggle we have had to wage for our present parliamentary form of government. I heard Magna Carta referred to rather slightingly this afternoon, and I also heard the Leader of the Opposition state what a great factor it has been in the development of our government throughout the ages. He said that Magna Carta might well be read by the Minister of Justice. I think it might well be read by all members of the house and by the people of

the country. Along with it we might read the Bill of Rights and the Petition of Rights. Those were all milestones on the hard road to freedom of parliament and the establishing of the rights of our people down through the years. Then if we wanted to read the .history of our own country, we might read of the struggle for responsible government here in Canada. We know that not only as to the parliament of Canada but in each of the provinces there was a difficult struggle by the people for responsible government.
To my mind it would be a great mistake for us in any way to weaken the supremacy of parliament especially in times such as these when we hold up ours as the type of government which protects the liberties of the people as opposed to the dictatorships in other countries.
I do not wish to say anything further on that matter, except that in this world today we are divided into two classes: those who believe in the dictatorship form of government, and we who believe in the democratic form of government. To my mind anything that weakens the democratic form of government is a step backward.
One argument has been presented time and time again-and this is my chief reason for rising to speak tonight, Mr. Chairman-by those speaking for the government. It has been argued that we have such a benevolent, benign form of government that, with the members representing that government, we could well trust our liberties to them and rest assured that nothing will be done to impair them. To my mind that is an exceedingly weak argument. I must confess that in my own province within the last year something occurred which I believe indicates that this government is not as kind and benevolent as it might be. I know there are many other people in my province who feel the same way as I do.
I refer to the arbitrary manner in which it was decided to take over 400 square miles of land in one of our good farming areas in the province of New Brunswick for a military training area. The matter was never brought before this parliament. The representatives of the people in that area were given absolutely no opportunity to say whether or not they wished that sort of thing done. It was never explained to them by the Minister of National Defence, the minister in charge, why it was necessary to take over the homes of these people, break up their societies and take away their churches. This was all done in an arbitrary manner by this government which, we are told today, we can trust with the liberties of the people.

When I asked that we be told by the Minister of National Defence why it was necessary to take over this area, I did not receive a satisfactory explanation. It may have been necessary. I am not saying that it was not. But I think the people of that area should have been told, and I think the matter should have been brought before parliament. But not one word has been said. However, it was done; and these people feel that it was an injustice. I also feel that a great injustice was done. Of course I know that if it had been explained to these people that it was absolutely necessary, they would have agreed to its being done. But in this day and age I say that an explanation should have been given to these people, and that their representatives in parliament should have had an opportunity to inquire into the matter.
Mr. Chairman, I am not going to prolong this debate, but I wished to make those few statements. Except in actual war, when the War Measures Act can be used, I believe parliament should be kept responsible in matters of this kind and not a few men in the government using arbitrary powers. We

I am giving only a layman's opinion, but that is my opinion. But there is something else. It is I think easily understandable why there has never been any such declaration made in the house. The executive government of Canada under the constitution is in the hands of the sovereign, and is exercised by the Governor General on the advice of his ministers who are sworn of the privy council, and who are bound by their oath not to disclose what goes on in their deliberations.
The Governor General acts on their advice, and they have the responsibility for all the acts that are performed. That is the constitutional position. No one of us is free to inform the house what takes place in our deliberations for the purpose of tendering advice to the Governor General on which he acts. He assures himself that he has the advice of his ministry and that the ministry, each and every member of it, will be responsible for the acts which he performs on their advice.

There was something that was a denial of the principles of parliamentary government. It is a dangerous power. We are not criticizing it because I know nothing of the circumstances.

I am opposed to secret orders. I remember one that was denied in parliament and afterwards admitted. The nearest it has ever come to being answered in this country was, as I pointed out, just after the first war. I am asking this question because one wonders how an order in council, such as the one in 1945, could have been passed by a cabinet of which the minister of justice was a member, and he could forget the existence of it. Mr. Chairman, I have not taken part in this debate up to this point, but the longer I have listened to it the more I have become convinced that we in this house and the people of Canada as a whole seem to be losing our consciousness of what individual liberty and individual rights are, and to be far too much inclined to think there is nothing out of the way in arbitrary power being given to the executive.
After listening to the discussion which has gone on today about secret orders and things of that sort, as to what arbitrary power the government may or may not exercise at its own discretion, it almost seems to me that the powers of the executive have completed a full circle. One would almost think that John Hampden had never lived and that we were back in the days of Charles I when it was held as a theory by a large number of people that the executive should be allpowerful and should exercise arbitrary rights

Emergency Powers Act without any rule or control as far as parliament or the representatives of the people were concerned.
The impact of the first and second world wars and of the conditions which have existed since the second world war has been ' such that a very large number of hon. members in this house and people throughout the country have been convinced that these arbitrary powers in the hands of the government are necessary. I think a large number of the speakers in this debate have shown that in order to meet any emergency which might arise it is not necessary for the government to have the arbitrary powers which they are seeking to secure by means of this particular bill.
If a real emergency develops, if a third world war should break out or anything else along that line, as has been pointed out time and again the War Measures Act is there and can be used; and this half-way war measures act, which gives the government power by order in council to take control of the economic life of this country or the affairs of any particular individual if it so desires, is not necessary.
The fact that the government say they are not going to do these things, that they are not going to abuse this power, is not important. If we as representatives of the people of Canada in this chamber actually do our job-I think perhaps it is one of our essential jobs-and protect the rights and liberties of the individual citizens of this country, then I think that we should deny to the government the power which they are asking for in this particular instance.
This makes me think of how far we have departed from what was more or less a universal feeling of independence, of individual liberty and so forth which existed in Great Britain and which was transplanted to this country and continued in existence here until the first great war. I think that type of independence of thought and personal freedom is exemplified best in the story of old Kelly of Silverstone who left a provision in his will that his grave was to be covered with sharp iron spikes so that those who came after would not be able to trample upon him even in death.
That spirit was more or less universal; individual liberty and freedom and the determination that the executive should not have arbitrary powers and, therefore, the right to trample on the individual. Unfortunately that spirit seems to have disappeared. If this parliament is to do its duty it should deny the government the powers they ask for and reassert that spirit which I think is essential 
if democratic institutions and individual freedom are to continue in this and other countries.

I would point out to him, however, that if the powers under the act are exercised while parliament is in session, under the terms of the act the order in council which results must be tabled within five days. It is open then to inspection by any member of the house and any member can by resolution take annulment proceedings in relation to it. I should think he would get that resolution on the order paper and have it debated and considered by parliament perhaps more rapidly than a bill to the same effect, introduced by the government, would come up for debate. My hon. friend will remember that when this matter was under discussion last
Emergency Powers Act year one of the members of the official opposition raised a question in relation to this resolution of annulment which is covered by section 2 (5) of the Emergency Powers Act, which reads:
If the Senate and House of Commons within a period of forty days, beginning with the day on which any regulation is laid before parliament in accordance with subsection four and excluding any time during which parliament is dissolved or prorogued or during which both the Senate and House of Commons are adjourned for more than four days, resolve that it be annulled, it shall cease to have effect.
The hon. member will recall that when we were considering that section of this act objection was taken by certain members of the official opposition to the fact that inasmuch as this would be a private member's resolution it would probably find its way to the bottom of the order paper and by a little tactical manoeuvring the government could arrange the orders of the day so that it would never be reached. On that occasion, after conferring with the Prime Minister, I came into the house and gave the undertaking on behalf of the government that in a case of that sort we would waive the house rules in order to give priority to this resolution of annulment.
I have no objection in the world to carrying my hon. friend's suggestion to my colleagues, but I do not think that for practical purposes it would make sufficient difference in the working of the legislation to be of much value. Let us consider that a certain subject matter is up for consideration and can be dealt with outside the terms of the Emergency Powers Act by the government bringing a bill into the house, on the one hand, or dealt with under the terms of the Emergency Powers Act by order in council, on the other hand. I suggest that while parliament was in session that matter could be dealt with by parliament, it could be disposed of or negated or annulled at least as quickly under the Emergency Powers Act as it could in the form of legislation introduced by the government. That being the case I think it is open to some doubt as to whether an amendment of that sort would really advance the interests of the opposition to any appreciable extent.

The Prime Minister stated his reasons quite clearly when he introduced the resolution leading up to the Emergency Powers Act in 1951. These were agreed to one by one by the Leader of the Opposition. That is, we did not want to create the impression by invoking the War Measures Act that war was inevitable, and frighten people and so on. Once we adopt that premise, that we do not wish to invoke the War Measures Act for these purposes at this time, then from that point on, if we are going to protect the people of Canada against such exigencies in the kind of conditions in which we live today, we must clothe the government with emergency powers to deal with exigencies which may arise and which we cannot now foresee.
It has so happened that during the past year no such exigency has arisen but an exigency may arise within one week or two weeks. Then where would my hon. friends of the opposition be if they voted against this measure?

That is no justification for this measure. The prerogative rights still exist. The second is freight cars. Is there any reason why prerogative rights should not exist in respect of matters such as that? Those are not emergencies arising out of the world situation. The need for freight cars in western Canada arises because we have an excess of wheat and require to have it marketed or removed, or to have an equalization of freight cars in the various communities. That can be done under the statute.
Finally the minister said: Suppose there was an invasion. Well, invasion is covered by the War Measures Act, which specifically states that the provisions of the last three sections-those are the pertinent ones-shall only be enforced during war, invasion or insurrection, real or apprehended.
What is this emergency? Surely after two or three days the minister could produce three better reasons than a repetition of box cars, invasion and election. We have had elections in the past and every government has been able to carry on.
I think the whole situation is best summed up, from the layman's point of view, in an editorial in the Ottawa Citizen dated February 20 entitled "What is an emergency?" That is a very pertinent question, and the longer I hear this argued by the Minister of Justice the more I am convinced that somehow there is something that he and the Prime Minister keep from parliament as completely as they are keeping this secret order, whatever it is; and in my opinion there is no provision in the regulations for filing or tabling such secret orders. The editorial reads: What is an emergency?
The House of Commons debate on the Emergency Powers Act has disclosed some dissatisfaction with its terms, and has failed to bring out a concept of emergency sufficiently well defined to prevent an abuse of power. The government itself, by a simple parliamentary majority, can declare a state

of emergency; and the present government has merely said that an emergency is by definition a state of "apprehended war".
It goes on to say:
The world being what it is, there would always be an excuse to ask for emergency powers, whether the threat to Canada's security is real or fancied. This cannot be what parliament wants.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, the minister can take parliament into his confidence and place before parliament reasons why this hungry government, greedy for power and used to power practically since its inception, and certainly since 1939, continues to grasp and hold power. It is one of the reasons why only the day before yesterday an outstanding leader of the Republican party in the United States used these words, and he was referring to the danger of granting powers:
Liberty may be destroyed by expenditure so great as to turn this country into a garrison state in time of peace . . . there are always conflicting dangers to liberty.
He said:
-usually freedom was lost because the people surrendered powers they had enjoyed perhaps because of some temporary emergency, without realizing how important it was to retain that freedom and how difficult it was to regain it.

When I listened today to the minister give the house his ideas of the attitude of this government to free enterprise, to the maintenance of free initiative, I thought of the speech which the Prime Minister made in Regina in 1949, during the election, when he was endeavouring to secure support from those who usually support socialism in Saskatchewan. Those were not the ideas of free enterprise that were placed before the house today. Taxation today socializes our country and denies freedom of enterprise. What is actually taking place in this country under the high rate of taxation is that ultimately the whole spirit of private enterprise is being undermined far beyond what is necessary to preserve integrity and initiative; and my hon. friend says that he and his party believe in free enterprise.
Yes, for the last few days they have taken some interest in the budget because they have

seen the results of the United States election and they are beginning to realize that the pendulum has swung. No longer may any government create a garrison state by socializing danger.
